report.source_text: Brain MRI including angiographic and gadolinium enhanced sequences, performed 4 months after the ophthalmic zoster infection, demonstrated the presence of subacute ischaemic changes in the right basal ganglia and the right cerebral peduncle. Narrowing of the supraclinoid segment of the right internal carotid artery (ICA) and the A1 segment of the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) and gadolinium enhancement in the vessel wall of the right ICA and ACA were noted (figure 1).

report.source_text: A follow-up MRI scan of the brain was performed 6 weeks after the MRI preceding hospitalisation and demonstrated persisting vasculitic vessel wall changes in the right ICA and the right ACA. Gadolinium enhancement was still present (see figure 1).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A woman in her 30s with relapsing-remitting MS and recent right ophthalmic zoster presented with new onset headache, right-sided occipital and retroorbital pain, photophobia, phonophobia, and right cheek twitches. Brain MRI performed 4 months after zoster demonstrated subacute ischemic lesions in the right basal ganglia and cerebral peduncle, with narrowing and gadolinium enhancement of the right internal carotid and anterior cerebral arteries. CSF analysis revealed positive VZV-DNA with normal cell counts and biochemistry, while extensive PCR testing excluded other infectious agents. Treatment with methylprednisolone, acyclovir, and aspirin was initiated, natalizumab was paused and later replaced by rituximab. Follow-up lumbar puncture after treatment showed negative VZV PCR and negative serologies for other infections. Follow-up MRI 6 weeks later showed persistent vasculitic vessel wall changes with gadolinium enhancement. The clinical presentation, imaging findings, CSF virological evidence, exclusion of other infections, and virological response after treatment support the diagnosis of cerebral zoster vasculopathy.
